judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's numeric claims are exact and I reproduced every one from the worksheet independently: a10 = 6 + 9(5) = 51; the linear rule 4n+7 gives a1 = 11 with 7 sitting at n = 0; 23 - 7 + 1 = 17 terms; 5 + 6(n-1) = 89 gives n = 15; the first twelve terms of 4, 9, 14, ... sum to (12/2)(4 + 59) = 378 against Priya's 408; 3, 10, 17, 24 has d = 7 and b = a1 - d = -4 so a20 = 136 against Dana's 143; and a5 through a20 of 3 + 4(n-1) is (16/2)(19 + 79) = 784 against the classmate's 735. The judge's design claims hold too - all eight items sit on an off-by-one, the three declared traps in verify.json (56, 16, 143, 408, 735) each reproduce the exact wrong number printed in the stem, and study_guide.pdf keeps steps, terms, the n=0 intercept and inclusive counts apart across its three sections. Where I part company is with a flawless instruction_following score, because the prompt says 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review' and this is a misconception-analysis sheet whose primary demanded response is a written diagnosis. Problem 1 prints 'Say in one sentence why Rosa takes one step too many'; problem 3 prints 'Explain what Milo's subtraction leaves out'; problem 5 prints 'Name the slip'. verify.json ids 1, 3 and 5 are a bare eval, a bare eval and a bare series respectively, with no manual entry anywhere except id 8. Separately, two concrete numeric slots go entirely unverified. Problem 6(a) says 'Test Dana's rule at n = 1 and say what it returns' and the answer key prints the result 10 ('7(1) + 3 = 10. That is a2, not a1'), yet verify.json id 6 contains only the a20 = 136 eval. Problem 7(a) says 'State how many terms the sum really contains' and the key prints 16 ('20 - 5 + 1 = 16 terms'), yet verify.json id 7 contains only the series total 784. The judge's own list of independently obtained values - 51, 11, 17, 15, 378, 136, 784 - is exactly the set of verify.json expecteds, which is the tell: the values 10 and 16 were never checked by anyone, machine or judge, because no entry declares them.

strengths_to_preserve: Every planted wrong answer is declared as a machine-checked trap whose value equals the number printed in the stem, and each is the specific off-by-one neighbour rather than a generic distractor: 56 is a11 with an extra d, 143 is a21, 16 is the gap count, and 735 falls short of 784 by 49, exactly one average term. The answer key says so out loud on problem 7: 'The shortfall of 49 is exactly the average term, so the wrong answer looks like a plausible sum - only the count betrays it.'

The n = 1 test is introduced in the worksheet header ('put n = 1 into any rule you write. A correct rule gives back the first term'), used as the Step 4 check in the answer key on problems 1, 2 and 6, and taught again as a bullet in study guide Skills 1 and 2. One diagnostic tool is threaded through all three documents instead of three unrelated tips.

Problem 4 gets two verify entries under one id - an eval of (v-a)/d + 1 = 15 for the index and a solve of 5 + 6*(n-1) - 89 = 0 for the equation the student is asked to write - so both printed sub-parts are bound. That is the decomposition problems 6 and 7 needed and did not get.

The worksheet header names the whole misconception family in one sentence before problem 1: 'Almost every wrong answer in this unit comes from one habit: counting terms when the rule counts steps.' The sheet then supplies the three faces of that habit (explicit rule, linear form, inclusive count) rather than eight variations of one.

root_causes.description: Verification was planned around each problem's terminal number, so a multi-part item is treated as covered once its final value verifies. On an error-analysis sheet this is the wrong unit: the named diagnosis is the skill under test and the intermediate value the student is explicitly asked to report (Dana's rule at n=1, the true term count) is a printed answer in its own right. verify.json declares one manual entry for the whole sheet, and the gate accepts it because the contract only requires at least one check per problem id.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 6 prints '(a) Test Dana's rule at n = 1 and say what it returns.' and answer_key.pdf answers it with 10; verify.json id 6 has exactly one entry, {type: eval, expr: d*n + (a - d), at: {a: 3, d: 7, n: 20}, expected: 136}.

worksheet.pdf problem 7 prints '(a) State how many terms the sum really contains.' and answer_key.pdf answers it with 16; verify.json id 7 has exactly one entry, the series 3 + 4*(n-1) from 5 to 20, expected 784.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers reads '6. 136' and '7. 784' - single values for two-part problems - while '4. 15, 15' correctly shows the two entries that problem 4 does declare.

worksheet.pdf problems 1, 3 and 5 each demand a written diagnosis before the number; verify.json ids 1, 3 and 5 carry no manual entry, and gate_log.txt still records the run as green with manual-review flags on the strength of id 8 alone.

improvements.title: Declare a verify entry for each lettered sub-part, including reported intermediate values like Dana's n=1 output and the true term count
improvements.proposed_change: Build a response-slot inventory from the worksheet source - one slot per lettered sub-part, plus one per conjoined request inside a sub-part - and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries plus manual entries bound to that id. For this case the fix is two added entries: under id 6, an eval of d*n + a at n = 1 with expected 10 (the value Dana's shifted rule returns, which is what part (a) asks for), and under id 7, an eval of q - p + 1 at p = 5, q = 20 with expected 16. Both then appear in the Quick Answers bank, so rows read '6. 10, 136' and '7. 16, 784' instead of hiding half the requested work.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture using curr-274's own problem 7 - prose with '(a) State how many terms the sum really contains. (b) Compute the correct sum.' bound to a verify.json id 7 holding only the series entry expecting 784. The slot-coverage gate must exit non-zero naming the uncovered part (a). Adding the eval q - p + 1 = 16 under the same id must make the fixture pass and must make the rendered bank row read '16, 784'.
improvements.expected_impact: On an error-analysis sheet the intermediate diagnostic value is often the whole point of the item; verifying it removes the possibility of a printed part-(a) answer drifting from the part-(b) computation. Across the run it closes the largest defect cluster.
improvements.risk: Sub-part detection from LaTeX prose will miscount when parts are written inline rather than as (a)/(b) markers, so the inventory needs both patterns and an explicit per-problem override; over-splitting could otherwise force authors into declaring trivially true checks.

improvements.title: Add manual entries for the named-diagnosis half of problems 1, 3 and 5
improvements.proposed_change: Gate on open-response constructions inside worksheet problem regions (Explain, Say in one sentence why, Name the slip, Describe, Justify, in your own words) and fail the build when the matching id has no manual entry. Here that means three added manual entries whose desc states what the reader should look for - for problem 1, that Rosa multiplied d by n rather than by n-1 because the first term costs no steps; for problem 3, that subtracting indices counts gaps rather than terms; for problem 5, that Priya used a1 + 12d as the twelfth term instead of a1 + 11d. The sheet's own instruction line, 'In each problem below: name the error in words first, then show corrected work', makes these mandatory responses rather than optional colour.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-274 problem 1's prose ('Say in one sentence why Rosa takes one step too many, then compute the correct 10th term') with verify.json id 1 holding only the eval expecting 51. The open-response gate must exit non-zero. Adding a manual entry under id 1 must make it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: Delivers the prompt's stated requirement on the sheet where it matters most - a misconception set whose declared instructional mode is diagnosis - and gives the teacher an explicit list of the four written diagnoses to read rather than one.
improvements.risk: Naming three more manual items raises the manual-review count on a sheet the machine currently reports as almost fully verified, which will look like a regression on any metric that rewards machine coverage; the gate summary needs to distinguish 'manual by design' from 'unverifiable by accident'.

case_summary: A genuinely excellent misconception set on sequence indexing - the ACCEPT is deserved and I found no mathematical error. All seven machine results reproduce (51, 11, 17, 15, 378, 136, 784), every planted wrong answer is declared as a trap whose value matches the number printed in the stem and is the exact off-by-one neighbour, and the n=1 test is taught in the header, used as a check throughout the key and re-taught in the study guide. Two coverage gaps sit under the perfect score. First, problems 6(a) and 7(a) print concrete numeric answers (10 and 16) that the answer key supplies but no verify entry declares - the judge's independently obtained list is precisely the set of verify expecteds, so those two values were checked by nobody. Second, the written diagnosis that the sheet's own directions make mandatory ('name the error in words first') is unflagged on problems 1, 3 and 5, so the only manual item declared is problem 8. Both are instances of the run's dominant systemic findings and neither disturbs the verdict.
